s01: Three jobs are ready for one machine: six minutes, two minutes, and one minute.
All the work takes nine minutes.
But the order changes how long the jobs wait to finish.
Run the longest first.
The jobs finish at six, eight, and nine minutes.
Their completion times add to twenty three.
Now run the shortest first.
They finish at one, three, and nine, adding to thirteen.
Why does the swap help?
Look at just a long job followed by a short one.
The first finishes after six minutes, and the second after eight.
Swap them: the first finish is now at two, while the final finish stays at eight.
Four minutes disappear from the total completion time.
In general, swapping an adjacent long job before a short job saves their length difference.
Everything after the pair starts at the same time as before.
Remove every reversed pair, and the jobs end up ordered from shortest to longest.
That minimizes the sum of completion times.
This assumes all jobs are ready, one machine, equal importance, and no setup delays or dependencies.
Deadlines and unequal importance can change the best order.
The amount of work did not shrink.
We changed the order so less of that work delays other jobs.

scenes.narration:
Three jobs are ready for one machine: six minutes, two minutes, and one minute. All the work takes nine minutes. But the order changes how long the jobs wait to finish.

Run the longest first. The jobs finish at six, eight, and nine minutes. Their completion times add to twenty three. Now run the shortest first. They finish at one, three, and nine, adding to thirteen.

Why does the swap help? Look at just a long job followed by a short one. The first finishes after six minutes, and the second after eight. Swap them: the first finish is now at two, while the final finish stays at eight. Four minutes disappear from the total completion time.

In general, swapping an adjacent long job before a short job saves their length difference. Everything after the pair starts at the same time as before. Remove every reversed pair, and the jobs end up ordered from shortest to longest. That minimizes the sum of completion times.

This assumes all jobs are ready, one machine, equal importance, and no setup delays or dependencies. Deadlines and unequal importance can change the best order. The amount of work did not shrink. We changed the order so less of that work delays other jobs.
